title: What are the four access modifiers and their exact visibility — public (everywhere), protected (same package + subclasses), default/package-private (same package only), private (same class only) — and which are legal on a top-level class (only public or package-private, NOT private/protected)?
shortTitle: What are the four access modifiers in Java?

s1_definition.profdef: Java has four access levels. `public` is visible everywhere, to any class in any package. `protected` is visible within the same package and additionally to subclasses in other packages. The default, also called package-private, which is the absence of any modifier, is visible only within the same package. `private` is visible only within the same class. For top-level classes and interfaces, only `public` and package-private are legal, because `private` and `protected` describe membership relationships that do not apply to a top-level type; a top-level class is either visible to the whole world via `public` or restricted to its own package by default.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, think of access modifiers as who can read a document. A `public` notice is pinned in the main lobby where any customer from any branch can read it. A `protected` memo is available to everyone in this branch and also to the branch's trainees who report to it, meaning the same package plus subclasses. A package-private file is visible only to staff in this one branch, nobody outside. A `private` note is in the manager's locked drawer, visible only inside that one office, meaning that one class. And for the building itself, a top-level class, it can either be open to the public or restricted to branch staff, but it makes no sense to call an entire building private or protected, which is why those are illegal on top-level classes.
s1_definition.oneliner: public is everywhere, protected is package plus subclasses, default is package-only, private is class-only — and top-level classes may be only public or package-private.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Java has four access levels. `public` is visible everywhere, to any class in any package. `protected` is visible within the same package and additionally to subclasses in other packages. The default, also called package-private, which is the absence of any modifier, is visible only within the same package. `private` is visible only within the same class. For top-level classes and interfaces, only `public` and package-private are legal, because `private` and `protected` describe membership relationships that do not apply to a top-level type; a top-level class is either visible to the whole world via `public` or restricted to its own package by default.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, think of access modifiers as who can read a document. A `public` notice is pinned in the main lobby where any customer from any branch can read it. A `protected` memo is available to everyone in this branch and also to the branch's trainees who report to it, meaning the same package plus subclasses. A package-private file is visible only to staff in this one branch, nobody outside. A `private` note is in the manager's locked drawer, visible only inside that one office, meaning that one class. And for the building itself, a top-level class, it can either be open to the public or restricted to branch staff, but it makes no sense to call an entire building private or protected, which is why those are illegal on top-level classes.

**One line to remember:** public is everywhere, protected is package plus subclasses, default is package-only, private is class-only — and top-level classes may be only public or package-private.

sections.s2_technical:
`public` members and types are accessible from any code anywhere, across all packages, as long as the containing type is itself accessible. This is for your intended API surface, like a service method clients call.

`protected` is the trickiest. A protected member is accessible within the same package, like package-private, and additionally in subclasses even if they are in a different package. But the cross-package subclass access has a subtle rule: a subclass can access a protected member through references of its own type or subtypes, not through an arbitrary reference of the parent type. Protected is meant for members that subclasses need to extend behavior, such as a hook method.

The default level, package-private, is what you get when you write no modifier at all. It restricts access to the same package. This is excellent for internal collaboration between classes that work together within one package, while hiding them from the outside world.

`private` restricts access to the declaring class only. Not even subclasses can see a private member. This is the foundation of encapsulation: fields are private and exposed, if at all, through controlled methods. Private members of the same top-level class are accessible across its nested classes too, because they share the same top-level class.

For top-level classes and interfaces, only `public` and package-private are allowed. A top-level class cannot be `private` or `protected`, because those modifiers express member-level relationships, such as being hidden inside a class or being inherited by subclasses, which have no meaning for a type that stands on its own at the package level. A senior nuance is that nested classes, by contrast, can use all four modifiers because they are members of their enclosing class. Another nuance is designing for the weakest access that still works: start private, widen only when necessary, because every bit of exposed surface is something external code can depend on and you must keep stable, which in a banking library is a real maintenance and security concern.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank exposes a transfer operation to external clients, hides internal balance fields completely, lets helper classes in the same package collaborate, and lets specialized account subclasses extend a validation hook. This maps exactly onto public, private, package-private, and protected.

Problem 2 — A developer tried to mark an entire top-level helper class as private and the code would not compile. This is exactly the rule that top-level classes may only be public or package-private.

Problem 3 — The team must show each modifier's reach with concrete access attempts. This is exactly what the demo illustrates.

The code has a `public` `Account` with a `private` balance, a `protected` validation hook, a package-private audit helper, and a `SavingsAccount` subclass using the protected hook, plus an `AccessModifierDemo` main class.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a SavingsAccount SAV2001 with a balance of 1,000,000, transferring 50000.

Step 1: Main creates a SavingsAccount. The constructor is public, so it is callable from this class in the same package and would be callable from anywhere.

Step 2: Main calls the public transfer method. Because it is public, it is part of the intended API surface and accessible everywhere.

Step 3: Inside transfer, the protected validate hook is called. Because SavingsAccount overrode it, the subclass version runs first calling super.validate, then adds the savings-specific limit check. Protected allowed the subclass to extend this behavior.

Step 4: The private balance field is updated inside the Account class. This is only possible because the code touching it is inside Account itself; main cannot touch balance directly because it is private.

Step 5: The package-private AuditHelper records the transfer. This works because AuditHelper and Account are in the same package; code outside the package could not use AuditHelper at all.

Step 6: Main reads the balance through the public getter, since it cannot read the private field directly. The result is logged, demonstrating each modifier's exact reach.

```text
INFO: SAV2001 transferred 50000, balance 950000.00
INFO: Balance via public getter = 950000.00
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  main (same package)
    │ public constructor
    ▼
  new SavingsAccount(SAV2001, 1,000,000)
    │ public transfer(50000) (callable everywhere)
    ▼
  validate(50000)  [protected hook]
    │ subclass override runs (same pkg + subclass access)
    ▼
  balance -= 50000  [private field, touched INSIDE Account only]
    │
    ▼
  audit.record(...)  [package-private helper, same package]
    │
    ▼
  getBalance()  [public]  → 950000.00

  main CANNOT: rajesh.balance (private) , top-level 'private class'
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — Visibility Matrix ═══

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Modifier        same   same    sub-     every  │
  │                 class  package class    where  │
  │ ─────────────────────────────────────────────│
  │ private     │
  │ package-private     │
  │ protected     │
  │ public     │

  Top-level class legality:
    public (visible to all packages)
    package-private (default, same package only)
    protected COMPILE ERROR
    private COMPILE ERROR
  (Nested classes MAY use all four — they are members.)

  Design rule (encapsulation):
    fields → private ; API → public ; hooks → protected ;
    helpers → package-private. Start narrow, widen only if needed.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Java has four access levels, and I think of them as concentric circles of visibility. Public is the widest: a public type or member is accessible from any code in any package, which is the intended API surface, like a service method that clients call. Protected is the next: it is accessible within the same package, and additionally in subclasses even across packages, so it is meant for extension points that subclasses need, like a validation hook. The default, which is package-private and is simply the absence of any modifier, restricts access to the same package, which is perfect for internal classes that collaborate but should stay hidden from the outside. And private is the narrowest: accessible only within the declaring class, which is the foundation of encapsulation, so fields are private and exposed only through controlled methods if at all.

For top-level classes and interfaces, only public and package-private are legal. A top-level class cannot be private or protected, because those two modifiers describe member-level relationships, being hidden inside a class or being inherited by subclasses, and those simply have no meaning for a type that stands on its own at the package level. A top-level class is either open to the whole world as public or confined to its own package by default. Nested classes are different, because they are members of their enclosing class, so they can use all four modifiers.

The one subtle point I always mention about protected is that cross-package subclass access is only through references of the subclass's own type, not through an arbitrary parent-typed reference.

In our banking code this maps cleanly. The transfer operation is public because clients call it, the balance field is private so no outside code can corrupt it, the audit helper is package-private so only classes in the same package collaborate with it, and the validation hook is protected so a savings-specific subclass can add its own transfer limit by extending it. My guiding design rule is to start with the weakest access that works, usually private, and widen only when there is a real need, because every bit of exposed surface becomes something external code can depend on and that I then have to keep stable and secure, which in a banking library is a genuine maintenance and security responsibility.
